title: When Is Knee Replacement Necessary? A Complete Guide
reviewedBy: Dr. Shahrukh Khan, MS Ortho, DNB Ortho (MAMC/NBE)

blocks.text: Total knee replacement (TKR), also called total knee arthroplasty, is a surgical procedure where damaged knee joint surfaces are replaced with metal and plastic implants. It is one of the most successful surgeries in modern medicine, restoring mobility to patients with severe knee arthritis.
Signs You May Need Knee Replacement

items: Severe knee pain that limits daily activities — walking, climbing stairs, rising from a chair
Moderate to severe knee pain at rest, even at night
Chronic knee inflammation and swelling unrelieved by medication
Knee deformity — bowing in or out
Failed non-surgical treatments for 6+ months (physiotherapy, injections, medications)

blocks.text: Most candidates are 60–80 years old, but age alone is not the criterion. Younger patients with severe post-traumatic arthritis or inflammatory joint disease may also benefit. Your orthopaedic surgeon will assess X-rays, clinical symptoms, and activity goals.

items: Physiotherapy and quadriceps strengthening
Weight loss (every kg lost reduces knee load by 4×)
Corticosteroid or hyaluronic acid injections
PRP (Platelet-Rich Plasma) therapy
Knee braces and walking aids

blocks.text: TKR takes 1.5–2 hours under spinal or general anaesthesia. You will be walking the next day with a physiotherapist. Hospital stay is 3–5 days. Most patients return to independent living in 4–6 weeks and full activity in 3–6 months.

items: Follow your physiotherapy programme religiously
Use ice packs to reduce swelling
Elevate leg when resting
Avoid high-impact activities (running, jumping) for 6 months
Annual follow-up with your surgeon

faqs.q: How long does a knee replacement last?
faqs.a: Modern implants last 15–25 years in most patients. Younger, active patients may eventually need revision surgery.
Immediate post-op pain is managed with multimodal analgesia. Most patients find the surgery pain far less than the chronic arthritis pain they lived with before.

faqs.q: Can both knees be replaced at the same time?
faqs.a: Simultaneous bilateral TKR is possible but carries higher risk. Most surgeons prefer staging them 6–12 weeks apart.

title: ACL Tear: Symptoms, Diagnosis & Treatment Options in Delhi

blocks.text: The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) is one of the four major ligaments of the knee, providing rotational stability. ACL tears are among the most common sports injuries, affecting athletes in football, cricket, basketball, and badminton.

items: Sudden change of direction (cutting movements)
Landing awkwardly from a jump
Direct collision or tackle
Sudden stop while running
A "pop" sound at the time of injury
Immediate swelling within hours
Severe pain and inability to continue activity
Feeling of knee "giving way"
Loss of full range of motion

blocks.text: Clinical examination (Lachman test, pivot shift test) combined with MRI confirms ACL tear and associated injuries (meniscus, cartilage, other ligaments).
RICE protocol, physiotherapy and knee bracing can suffice for partial tears or patients with low activity demands. However, chronic instability increases meniscus damage risk.

Arthroscopic ACL reconstruction uses a graft (hamstring or patellar tendon) to recreate the torn ligament. It is a day-care or overnight procedure. Return to sport typically takes 9–12 months with proper rehabilitation.

items: Week 1–2: Swelling control, straight leg raises
Week 4–6: Stationary cycling, strengthening
Month 3: Jogging
Month 6: Sport-specific training
Month 9–12: Return to competitive sport

faqs.q: Can I walk with an ACL tear?
faqs.a: Yes, many patients can walk after an ACL tear once swelling subsides, but the knee may feel unstable, especially during pivoting activities.

faqs.q: Do all ACL tears need surgery?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Partial tears in low-demand patients can be managed conservatively. Complete tears in athletes or active individuals generally require reconstruction.

title: Hip Replacement Surgery: Complete Patient Guide

blocks.text: Total hip replacement (THR) removes the damaged ball and socket of the hip joint and replaces it with prosthetic components. It is one of the most transformative surgeries, eliminating severe hip pain and restoring walking ability.
Conditions That Lead to Hip Replacement

items: Osteoarthritis (most common)
Rheumatoid arthritis
Avascular necrosis (bone death due to poor blood supply)
Hip fracture in elderly patients
Childhood hip dysplasia causing adult arthritis

blocks.text: THR takes 1.5–2 hours. The surgeon removes the worn femoral head and acetabular cartilage, then fits metal, ceramic, or polyethylene implants. Modern techniques (anterior approach) allow faster recovery with less muscle damage.

items: Day 1–2: Standing and walking with a walker
Week 2–4: Walking independently indoors
Month 1–3: Return to most daily activities
Month 3–6: Driving, light sport, stairs without aid
Avoid crossing legs for 6 weeks
Use raised toilet seats and grab bars
Sleep with a pillow between knees initially
No low sofas or bending past 90 degrees (posterior approach)

faqs.q: How long does a hip replacement last?
faqs.a: 90% of hip replacements last 15–20 years. Highly cross-linked polyethylene and ceramic bearings in modern implants can last 25+ years.

faqs.q: Is hip replacement done under general anaesthesia?
faqs.a: Most surgeons prefer spinal (regional) anaesthesia — you are awake but numb from the waist down, with less risk and faster recovery than general anaesthesia.

title: Stroke Warning Signs: FAST and When to Call an Ambulance

blocks.text: Every minute of stroke, 1.9 million brain neurons die. Prompt action — calling an ambulance immediately — is the single most important thing a bystander can do. Treatment within the "golden window" (4.5 hours for clot-busting, 24 hours for thrombectomy) can restore function completely.

items: F — Face drooping: One side of the face droops; asymmetric smile
A — Arm weakness: One arm weak or numb; cannot hold both arms raised equally
S — Speech difficulty: Slurred, garbled, or inability to speak or understand
T — Time to call 112: If ANY of these signs, call immediately
B — Balance: Sudden loss of balance or coordination
E — Eyes: Sudden vision loss or double vision in one or both eyes
Ischaemic (85%): Blood clot blocks a brain artery. Treated with tPA (clot-buster) or mechanical thrombectomy
Haemorrhagic (15%): Blood vessel bursts in or around the brain. Surgical treatment in selected cases
High blood pressure (most important) — target <130/80 mmHg
Atrial fibrillation — anticoagulation prevents embolic stroke
Diabetes and high cholesterol
Smoking — doubles stroke risk
Obesity and physical inactivity

faqs.q: Can stroke happen at any age?
faqs.a: Yes — while stroke risk increases with age, 10–15% of strokes occur in people under 45. Young stroke causes include cardiac emboli, thrombophilia, and cervical artery dissection.

title: Brain Tumour Warning Signs You Should Never Ignore

blocks.text: Brain tumours can be primary (starting in the brain) or secondary/metastatic (spreading from elsewhere). They are classified as benign (non-cancerous) or malignant (cancerous). Early detection significantly improves outcomes.

Brain tumour headaches are often worst in the morning (increased intracranial pressure when lying flat), worsen progressively, and are associated with nausea or vomiting. A new headache pattern or a headache that is "the worst of your life" warrants urgent evaluation.
A first-ever seizure in an adult (especially after age 30) requires brain imaging to exclude a tumour. The type of seizure can point to tumour location.

items: Weakness or numbness on one side of the body
Vision disturbances (double vision, field defects)
Speech difficulties — slurred speech or word-finding problems
Balance and coordination problems
Hearing loss (acoustic neuroma)

blocks.text: Memory problems, confusion, personality change, or mood disturbance — especially if new and progressive — can indicate a frontal or temporal lobe tumour.
MRI brain with gadolinium contrast is the standard investigation. CT scan is faster in emergencies. Biopsy confirms the tumour type — essential for treatment planning.

items: Surgery (craniotomy or keyhole): primary treatment for accessible tumours
Radiotherapy: adjuvant or definitive for certain tumours
Chemotherapy (e.g., temozolomide for glioblastoma)
Stereotactic radiosurgery (Gamma Knife): for small/deep tumours

faqs.a: No — benign tumours (meningioma, pituitary adenoma, acoustic neuroma) are often curable with surgery. Malignant tumours carry variable prognosis depending on grade and type.

title: Complete Vaccination Schedule for Children in India 2026

blocks.text: Why Vaccination Is the Most Cost-Effective Healthcare Intervention

Vaccines prevent 2–3 million deaths globally every year. India's National Immunisation Schedule (NIS) has been updated in 2026 with new additions. Keeping your child up-to-date with vaccinations is the single most important thing you can do to protect their health.

items: Birth: BCG (TB), OPV-0, Hepatitis B-1
6 weeks: DTwP-1, IPV-1, HepB-2, Hib-1, Rotavirus-1, PCV-1
10 weeks: DTwP-2, IPV-2, Hib-2, Rotavirus-2, PCV-2
14 weeks: DTwP-3, IPV-3, Hib-3, Rotavirus-3, PCV-3
6 months: HepB-3, OPV-1
9 months: MMR-1, OPV-2, Vitamin A (1st dose)
12 months: Hepatitis A-1, Typhoid conjugate
15 months: MMR-2, Varicella-1, PCV booster
18 months: DTwP Booster-1, OPV Booster, Hib Booster, Hepatitis A-2
2 years: Typhoid booster
4–6 years: DTwP Booster-2, OPV Booster, MMR-3, Varicella-2
9–14 years (girls): HPV vaccine (cervical cancer prevention)
10 years: Tdap, Meningococcal
Influenza (annual, especially for children with asthma or heart disease)
Pneumococcal (beyond NIS)
Meningococcal (for high-risk children)

faqs.q: My child missed some vaccines — is it too late?
faqs.a: No — catch-up vaccination is always possible. Our paediatrician will create a personalised catch-up schedule. Vaccination at any age is better than not vaccinating.

Yes — vaccines undergo the most rigorous safety testing of any medical product. Serious adverse events are extremely rare (1 in millions). The risk of the disease is always far greater than the risk of the vaccine.

title: Fever in Children: When to Worry & When to Wait

blocks.text: Fever (temperature ≥38°C / 100.4°F) is the body's natural immune response to infection. It is not an illness itself — it is a sign that the immune system is working. Most fevers in children are caused by viral infections and resolve in 2–5 days without specific treatment.

items: Rectal (most accurate for infants): ≥38°C = fever
Axillary (underarm): ≥37.5°C = fever (0.5°C less than rectal)
Oral: ≥37.8°C = fever
Forehead / ear strips: Less accurate — use for screening only

blocks.text: When to Seek Immediate Medical Care

items: Any fever in a baby <3 months (even low-grade) — emergency
Fever >39.4°C in children under 2 years
Fever lasting >5 days at any age
Fever with rash, stiff neck, severe headache, light sensitivity (possible meningitis)
Fever with difficulty breathing, persistent vomiting, or dehydration
Child very difficult to wake, unusually confused or limp
Fever with a febrile seizure
Paracetamol: 15 mg/kg every 4–6 hours
Ibuprofen (>6 months): 10 mg/kg every 6–8 hours
Encourage fluids — fever causes fluid loss
Light clothing — do not bundle up
Tepid sponging: lukewarm water (not cold/ice)

faqs.q: Do I need to reduce every fever?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Fever serves an immune function. Treat fever if child is uncomfortable, not just because the thermometer reads high. The number alone does not determine treatment — the child's overall appearance does.

title: CBC Blood Test Explained: What Each Value Means

blocks.text: A Complete Blood Count (CBC) is the most commonly ordered blood test, providing a comprehensive snapshot of your blood's cellular components. It is used to diagnose anaemia, infections, inflammatory conditions, blood cancers, and monitor treatment response.
Normal: Men 4.5–5.9 million/μL; Women 4.0–5.2 million/μL. Low (anaemia): fatigue, pallor, breathlessness. High (polycythaemia): increased clot risk.
Normal: Men 13–17 g/dL; Women 12–15 g/dL; Children varies by age. Low = anaemia (iron deficiency most common; also B12, thalassaemia). Hb below 8 g/dL is severe anaemia.
Small (microcytic, MCV <80): iron deficiency or thalassaemia. Large (macrocytic, MCV >100): B12 or folate deficiency, liver disease, medications.
High (leukocytosis): infection, inflammation, stress, steroids, rarely leukaemia. Low (leukopenia): viral infections, medications, immune disorders.
High (neutrophilia): bacterial infection, steroids. Low (neutropenia): risk of serious infection below 0.5 × 10⁹/L.
Low (thrombocytopenia): dengue, ITP, bone marrow problem, medications. High (thrombocytosis): reactive (infection, iron deficiency) or rarely bone marrow disorder.

faqs.q: Do I need to fast for a CBC test?
faqs.a: No — CBC does not require fasting. However, if your CBC is part of a panel that includes fasting tests (lipid profile, FBS), fast for the entire panel.
An abnormal CBC (very high WBC, very low platelets, abnormal-looking cells on peripheral smear) raises suspicion and prompts further investigation. Diagnosis requires bone marrow biopsy.

title: HbA1c Test: What It Is, Normal Range & What It Means for Diabetes

blocks.text: HbA1c (glycated haemoglobin) measures the percentage of haemoglobin in your red blood cells that has glucose attached to it. Because red blood cells live for approximately 3 months, HbA1c reflects your average blood sugar level over the past 2–3 months — making it far more informative than a single blood glucose reading.

items: Normal (non-diabetic): Below 5.7%
Prediabetes: 5.7%–6.4%
Diabetes: 6.5% and above
Diabetic target (on treatment): Below 7.0% (general); <8.0% for elderly or high hypoglycaemia risk
No fasting required
Not affected by a single day's diet
Shows average control, not just the moment of testing
Better predictor of diabetic complications
Haemoglobin disorders (sickle cell disease, thalassaemia) — false results
Severe anaemia or recent blood transfusion
Haemolytic anaemia — artificially low HbA1c
Iron deficiency — can falsely elevate HbA1c

faqs.q: How often should I check my HbA1c?
faqs.a: If well-controlled (below target): every 6 months. If recently changed medication or poorly controlled: every 3 months. New diabetics: every 3 months until stable.

title: Thyroid Function Tests: TSH, T3, T4 — What Your Results Mean

blocks.text: Thyroid disorders affect 1 in 10 Indians — women are 5–8× more likely to be affected. Hypothyroidism (underactive) and hyperthyroidism (overactive) have vastly different symptoms but both significantly impact quality of life and — if untreated — can cause serious cardiac, bone, and metabolic problems.
TSH (Thyroid Stimulating Hormone) — the MOST IMPORTANT screening test

Produced by pituitary gland to stimulate thyroid. Normal: 0.4–4.0 mIU/L (lab-specific ranges vary). High TSH → thyroid underactive → HYPOTHYROIDISM. Low TSH → thyroid overactive → HYPERTHYROIDISM. TSH alone is sufficient to screen for thyroid disease in most cases.
The main hormone secreted by the thyroid. Normal: 12–22 pmol/L. Confirmed LOW FT4 + HIGH TSH = Primary hypothyroidism. Confirmed HIGH FT4 + LOW TSH = Hyperthyroidism.
Active form of thyroid hormone (T4 converts to T3 in tissues). Less useful for routine screening; helpful for T3 toxicosis and monitoring hyperthyroid treatment.

items: Anti-TPO antibodies: marker of Hashimoto's thyroiditis (commonest cause of hypothyroidism)
TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb): Graves' disease (commonest cause of hyperthyroidism)

faqs.q: Do I need to fast for thyroid tests?
faqs.a: No fasting is required for TSH, FT4 or FT3. However, biotin supplements (found in hair/nail supplements) can interfere — stop biotin 2 days before thyroid testing.

faqs.q: My TSH is slightly high — do I need medication?
faqs.a: Subclinical hypothyroidism (mildly elevated TSH with normal FT4) in otherwise well patients is often monitored rather than treated immediately. Treatment is generally recommended if TSH >10, or if symptomatic, pregnant, or trying to conceive.
